notes: Main kinds of disagreement and resolutions. (1) unit_stance was the largest source: the coders often used `require` or `permit` for must-do duties such as citing, disclosing or removing PII. I used the CODEBOOK definitions: `require` only where AI use itself is required, `permit` for conditions on permitted use (disclosure, citation), `restrict` for limits on use or data, `neutral` for duties about outputs, enforcement and rationale. I also applied this to a few units where the coders agreed (doc 1 syllabus-statement requirement and citation duty, doc 3 citation), recorded in resolution_why. (2) Phase: general vs a time-bound phase for principles and definitions, settled by whether the sentence names a point in the course. (3) Actor: all vs admin or instructor, settled by who the sentence binds (the institution's own vision statements are admin; 'researchers' are all). (4) policy_type: P56/P04 and other near types, settled against the covers text (P63 vs P122 for faculty grants -> P63; P101 vs P73 for human oversight of evaluations -> P73; accreditation UNCOVERED vs P76 -> P76; P09 vs P78 for syllabus content -> P09; P36 vs P01 for 'may be considered a violation' -> P36). (5) Modality: bare imperatives and 'will' commitments -> must; hedged 'may be considered' -> informs. (6) Units found by only one coder: kept 5 from A and 8 from B (separate rules in adjacent sentences, separate clauses, or real statements); dropped 4 from A on doc 1 (vision-aim clause already in a coded sentence, partnership news item, two resource-link titles from a list already represented by one unit). In three places the aligner paired adjacent but different sentences; I counted them as unmatched and kept both units. Two coder pairs were crossed in order and were re-paired by passage.
